desc:
An array is a mountain if it has at least 3 elements and there is an index p with 0 < p < length - 1 such that the values strictly increase up to p and strictly decrease after it. Both slopes must have at least one step, so the peak is never the first or last element.

Return the smallest number of elements you must delete from nums so that what remains is a mountain. The input is guaranteed to allow this. For nums = [2, 1, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3, 1] the answer is 3 (keep 1, 5, 6, 3, 1).
constraints: A mountain can be obtained by deleting some elements
hints: Keeping as many elements as possible is the same as finding the longest mountain subsequence. Fix the peak index p.
Let inc[p] be the longest strictly increasing subsequence ending at p, and dec[p] the longest strictly decreasing subsequence starting at p. A peak is only valid if both are at least 2.

The longest mountain through p keeps inc[p] + dec[p] - 1 elements. Take the best valid p; the answer is n minus that. Compute inc and dec in O(n log n) with the tails technique, or in O(n<sup>2</sup>) with a double loop.
editorial: The elements to keep must form a mountain, so we want the longest mountain subsequence. Choose its peak at index p. The part left of the peak is a strictly increasing subsequence ending at p; the part right of it is a strictly decreasing subsequence starting at p, and the two can be chosen independently. The best choices have lengths inc[p] and dec[p], giving a mountain of inc[p] + dec[p] - 1 elements.

The only subtlety is the requirement of both slopes: a peak with inc[p] = 1 (nothing before it) or dec[p] = 1 (nothing after it) is not a mountain, so those indices must be skipped. This is the usual trap; a plain 'longest bitonic' formula would wrongly allow a sorted array to be kept completely.
Compute inc and dec with the LIS tails technique (bisect_left for strictness) in O(n log n), then scan all valid p. The answer is n - max(inc[p] + dec[p] - 1). Memory is O(n).
